title: Errors, tests and explicit input contracts
outcome: Validate scientific inputs, test expected failures and preserve unexpected errors instead of turning them into successful results.
key_terms: The exception thrown when a caller supplies an unacceptable argument, such as an empty vector where data are required.
The exception thrown when a numeric value lies outside a function's mathematical domain, such as `sqrt(-1.0)` on real inputs.
A `@testset` block from the `Test` standard library that groups related `@test` checks and reports their results together.
An input at the edge of the valid domain, such as zero or one element, where validation and off-by-one mistakes appear.
Calling `rethrow()` inside a `catch` block reraises the current exception with its original backtrace after local handling.
approach: `finite_mean` enforces its contract in order: reject an empty vector with `ArgumentError`, reject any nonfinite value with `DomainError`, then return `mean`. `outcome` converts only those two promised failures into a `:rejected` named tuple and rethrows anything else, so a programming defect still stops the run.

exercises.title: Keep valid zero
exercises.expected: The result is the valid number 0.
exercises.hint: Do not confuse a zero result with rejection.
exercises.answer: The input satisfies the contract and its arithmetic mean happens to be zero.
exercises.why: `[-1, 1]` is nonempty and finite, so both guards pass and `mean` returns 0.0, a legitimate result rather than a rejection signal.
exercises.wrong: Using zero as a sentinel for invalid input would make this valid mean indistinguishable from a rejected batch in any downstream table.
exercises.verify: Worked example A asserts `finite_mean([-1, 1]) == 0`; pass the same vector through `outcome` and expect status `:ok`.

exercises.title: Reject empty input
exercises.task: Call the helper on an empty vector.
exercises.expected: ArgumentError identifies the missing observation requirement.
exercises.answer: A fabricated zero would hide the absence of evidence.
exercises.why: `isempty(values)` is checked first, so `Float64[]` raises `ArgumentError` before `mean` could divide by a count of zero.
exercises.wrong: Returning 0.0 for empty input invents an observation, and averaging that into a report weights a group that has no data.
exercises.verify: Assert `@test_throws ArgumentError finite_mean(Float64[])`, then check that `outcome(Float64[]).reason` mentions observation.

exercises.title: Reject nonfinite values
exercises.task: Include NaN or Inf in the input.
exercises.hint: Check the numeric domain before aggregation.
exercises.answer: Nonfinite values need a declared policy rather than silent propagation into a report.
exercises.why: `all(isfinite, values)` fails for NaN or Inf, so the function throws `DomainError` and names the offending vector.
exercises.wrong: Letting NaN flow into `mean` yields NaN, which then compares false with everything and quietly drops out of later filters.
exercises.verify: The reference asserts `@test_throws DomainError finite_mean([NaN])` and `outcome([Inf]).status == :rejected`.

exercises.title: Preserve an unexpected error
exercises.task: Pass a value for which the required methods do not exist.
exercises.expected: The unexpected method error is rethrown.
exercises.hint: Catch only the failures that the boundary promises to handle.
exercises.answer: A broad catch can hide a programming defect behind a normal-looking outcome.
exercises.why: A vector of strings passes the empty check, then `isfinite` has no string method, so `MethodError` escapes and `outcome` rethrows it.
exercises.wrong: A bare `catch` returning `:rejected` for every error would label a type mistake in the caller as bad data and hide the bug.
exercises.verify: The reference checks `@test_throws MethodError finite_mean(["not numeric"])`; example B also shows `outcome(nothing)` rethrowing.

exercises.title: Test independently
exercises.task: Validate a result using a hand calculation and a limiting case.
exercises.expected: The assertion has an independent basis.
exercises.hint: Avoid copying the same implementation expression.
exercises.answer: Different reasoning paths reduce the chance that code and test share one unnoticed error.
exercises.why: A hand calculation such as (1 + 2 + 3) / 3 = 2 and a limiting case like a single value `[7]` come from reasoning separate from the code.
exercises.wrong: Writing the expected value as `sum(v) / length(v)` copies the implementation, so the test passes even if both share a mistake.
exercises.verify: Keep `finite_mean([7]) == 7` from the reference and add one hand-derived mean with its arithmetic written in a comment.

exercises.title: Report rejected rows
exercises.task: Aggregate valid outcomes from a mixed input stream.
exercises.expected: Retain counts and reasons for rejected rows.
exercises.answer: Selection through validation can change the target population and should remain visible.
exercises.why: Mapping `outcome` over rows yields `:ok` and `:rejected` tuples, so valid values and rejection reasons can be counted separately.
exercises.wrong: Averaging only the successful values and printing that mean alone hides how many rows were excluded and why.
exercises.verify: Report the counts of `:ok` and `:rejected` beside the mean and confirm they add up to the number of input rows.

checks_note: The checks follow the two error styles in the lesson. `finite_mean` returns 7 for `[7]` and throws `DomainError` for NaN, while `outcome` packages the same decision as a status, so `[Inf]` yields `:rejected` without an exception. A string input fails with `MethodError` before any arithmetic, showing that dispatch rejects it first. The last line accepts `0.1 + 0.2` rounding because it only asks for a finite result.
